Catch Me If You Can was, unfortunately, a very boring watch for me. For a a very long time it felt like nothing was really happening and once things finally picked up, the film became repetitive. I genuinely don’t understand the hype around it. Sometimes it feels like its popularity is carried by Leonardo DiCaprio being in it more than the story itself. The ending was the strongest part and definitely left a better impression than the rest of the film. What made it even harder to buy, was that it’s based on a true story. I just couldn’t believe Frank managed to get away with everything he did for so long it felt far too unbelievable. Plus despite Frank being the protagonist and going through so much, I never felt emotionally connected to him, none of the shit he went through really affected me. Except maybe when he flushed himself through the toilet :(

Una d'algunes de les que tenia pendents i ni m'ha impressionat ni m'ha decebut. No considero que sigui una obra aclaparadora perquè no té res que la faci sorprenent més enllà d'una història trepidant i excel·lentment narrada. Intueixo que això és el que provoca sensacions. Spielberg agafa la biografia de Frank Abagnale , un precoç estafador estatunidenc que causaria impacte a la societat nord-americana amb la seva habilitat per l'engany. Una cosa és tenir un bon material de fons i l'altra saber portar-lo a la pantalla gran d'una forma completament brillant. Em congratula veure que Spielberg ho aconsegueix i, aparentment, sense cap mena de dificultat. Com a espectador no necessites reflexionar en excés o estar atentíssim per no perdre't el mínim detall. És una pel·lícula que es gaudeix sola: té un ritme lleuger, molt viu i extremadament agradable. La crònica no és monòtona i presenta uns girs i ocurrències que traspassen el predictible. M'agrada pensar que tota història està precedida d'un missatge de fons, d'una intenció clara independentment de l'entreteniment. Aquí se'm complica més identificar-ho, no perquè no hi sigui, sinó perquè crec que se li dona menys importància. La inevitabilitat del protagonista per deixar de mentir és un tret que pot abordar certes reflexions, però per mi no arriba a una profunditat digna de menció. Frank Abagnale (un genial Leonardo DiCaprio ) fa de la mentida patològica el seu modus operandi, un comportament persistent i compulsiu que forma part de la seva identitat. Una característica visiblement present també en el seu pare (interpretat per un grandiós Christopher Walken ) que ens deixaria una metàfora molt il·lustrativa que després heretaria el seu fill: "Two little mice fell in a bucket of cream. The first mouse quickly gave up and drowned. The second mouse, he wouldn't quit. He struggled so hard that eventually he churned that cream into butter and crawled out." Frank Abagnale Sr. viu constantment en un món envoltat de fantasia, s'obliga ell mateix a viure en un ordre construït per les seves autocomplaences i vol sempre anar per un camí que no li correspon i no es pot permetre. Quan la realitat se li fa evident l'única cosa que sembla aprendre és traslladar les responsabilitats als seus perseguidors. La metàfora li serveix per arrossegar al seu fill amb el niu de l'adoctrinament. Projecta el seu ego i deixa de fer-li de pare per fer-li d'animador quan les seves decisions són notòriament reprovables. Aquest suport fa que Frank Abagnale Jr. sigui una versió "millorada" del que és el seu pare. Ell ja no menteix per benefici, menteix perquè li proporciona plaer i fa que la resta de mortals l'admirin. Utilitza constantment als qui l'envolten com a mers instruments a punt per ser manipulats. Tot això l'acaba convertint en un home exteriorment idíl·lic, però interiorment desert. Un narcisisme que, poc a poc i amb l'ajuda d'un agent de l'FBI (Tom Hanks), aconsegueix gestionar. Sí, és un relat de superació personal. No obstant l'anterior, la conclusió, amb tot el que comporta, és el postre en aquest menú de Spielberg .

I'll admit however, searching for details about the real Frank Abignale has soured my enjoyment somewhat. The film does only say it was "inspired" by true events. However, it's still a common misconception that the film is or was at least based on a true story, when many of Frank's claims have been disputed as far back as the late 70s. Meanwhile, his real exploits include allegedly impersonating a doctor to sexually assault Pan Am flight attendants. The film not only supports his lies, but glorifies and exonerates him to an almost comical degree. The real Frank even gets a cutesy cameo. Unlike another, similarly false movie based on "true" events, "21", this film doesn't even give Frank an alias to allow any reasonable separation. It concludes with a wall of wrap-up text to update the audience on his career and assure us that Frank and Tom Hanks' fictional FBI agent remained good friends. Somewhat suspiciously, when it comes to his check fraud, the film goes to great lengths to explain the mechanics of how the scheme works. When it comes to his lengthy impersonations, the film largely glosses over these. As if impersonating a head pediatrician for a year is too ludicrous to even portray. We never see him in an operating room, a cockpit, or a courtroom for more than a minute each. Much of it seems to rely of a lot of adult women being easily manipulated or too horny for this 17 year old to see through him. I don't know if the book cares to elaborate further, but I have my suspicions. Still, it's a highly entertaining, if not slightly frustrating film to engage with.

Spielberg brilliantly sets the tone of Frank’s exploits as a game show, appropriating the very silly, very American craving for attention and flair for the spectacular(ly convoluted). I wonder how early on he knew it was all a ruse. “Knock knock.” I've had many conversations with composers & friends about how much they were struck by John Williams’s opening credits music. The very first time at the cinema, I recall beaming at the screen – feeling the love for the Pink Panther movies & Henry Mancini. Instead of deploying his usual massive, brass-heavy orchestra, Williams curated a lean, intimate chamber ensemble focused on precise textures, including: - Solo Alto Saxophone: Played by renowned session musician Dan Higgins, the saxophone acts as the primary "voice". Its slinky, fluid lines mimic the nimble movements of Frank Abagnale Jr.. - Mallet Percussion (Vibraphone & Marimba): The vibraphone provides the characteristic mid-century jazz shimmer, while the woody timbre of the marimba anchors the lower rhythms. They frequently play interlocking triplet patterns together. - Tactile Sound Effects: The arrangement famously integrates finger snaps & human "shushes" directly into the percussion mix, instantly grounding the track in the jazz-club aesthetic of the era. Williams deliberately channelled the style of his own musical youth - when he was known as a jazz pianist named "Johnny Williams" - while paying homage to 1960s movie music masters like Mancini. And then this is my favourite Tom Hanks performance in a Spielberg movie. Hanratty is a straight man in a straight career, crunching numbers on criminals who have created new ways to crunch numbers. He is the perfect opposite of Frank. Hanks has physicality, but it’s a contained performance – all in the accent, stiff jaw & posture. “Next slide, please. Next slide, please.” Also have to give my respects to the twinkle in the eyes of Christopher Walken. The father/ son tale at the heart of this is pure Spielberg tragedy. Quite adjacent to the real-life tale, as is much of the movie – but those random restaurant meetings are just heart-breaking to watch. Thank goodness they never filmed his Central Station death as was planned. DiCaprio’s raw pain at learning about the death after-the-fact is pain enough. I haven’t loved anything by Spielberg as much in the quarter decade since. Part of my ‘Spielberg Phase’ of a LetterBoxd Review Catch-Up. Viewed courtesy of the Home Library

Where are you going, Frank? The thesis of this film becomes so many things about what we do when our dreams are crushed or we feel like we are put in between a rock and a hard place. The opening scenes feel so vividly like real memories I have of proud moments in my parents lives and moments when I idolized my parents relationship at a young age. The immediate subversion of this idolization into an unhealthy view of how to “win” at life and how to cheat everyone around you I think is what always attaches me to Frank early. I  have this deep sadness when I witness moments where parents do things for their kids, make sacrifices or life change, and the child doesn’t understand and becomes ungrateful or upset. I don’t know why making it by the best a person can just hits me deeply but this and Pursuit of Happyness are examples of movies that stick a shovel in my gut. Selling the families car and pancakes on birthdays from Frank Sr transform into christmases alone and literal prison time for Frank Jr. The movie paints these mirrors and patterns so wonderfully as personal and emotional moments coming from Frank and his reactions to these situations, it’s not just the consequences but the quiet sadness of the facade shattering. I think that’s what makes Frank Jr so engaging, his granger feels so fantastical and impossibly silly but simultaneously desperate, unexplainable, and tragic by the end. It’s never a hero story, but one where we try to understand him in his lows and highs. There is so much of Spielbergs real life in this family routine, his mother cheating specifically became very familiar.  But most importantly this movie is very obviously not a biopic about Frank Abagnale, it’s a movie about a man who stays a kid for much too long and pushes his luck because he’s scared of conflict. And as much as I’d love to say I don’t relate to that, this movie feels uncomfortable in its lies because i have tried to avoid so many scary things in my life, and im still very early at learning that it won’t kill me to go through things, not around. I think something else interesting here is how Frank and Carl both start as outsiders. People who have to make concessions to those around them to gather favor. They are not so different. We get these conversations between them full of acusations and and jabs because they are both insecure about the same things. It’s a wonderful structure of the ring spreading out and then closing back in on each of them. Visually, this movie more than any Spielberg makes me feel all of its wider lenses. The prevalent use of hand held camera in this movie also emphasizes this effect, scenes ending with an empty room that feels round and swimming, and the blocking feels that much more like a dance than shapes passing. I saw this movie very early in my life and it is still such a rich little roller coaster I like to hop on sometimes. It always surprises me.
